opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is simply that embodied intelligence has a data problem that language models never had. When large language models scaled, they could draw on decades of text already on the internet. Nobody had to create that data for the models. For robots, there's no equivalent. There's no internet of physical interaction: no huge archive of a hand grasping a cup, the force it applies, how the object slips, what the camera sees at each moment, and how the motor commands map to all of that.

So the default today is to collect real-world data, through teleoperation or putting robots into homes and factories. That data is extremely valuable, and I don't think we'll ever fully replace it. But it's slow and expensive, and it's hard to cover the long tail. One operator can gather maybe a few hundred good demonstrations a day. If you want a robot to handle thousands of objects, different lighting, cluttered tables, deformable things like clothes or cables, and all the failure cases, the numbers just don't add up. You'd need orders of magnitude more data than any company can collect by hand.

Synthetic data changes the economics. In simulation or with generative methods, you can vary the scene, the object geometry, the materials, the physics parameters, and the camera viewpoint almost freely, and you can run it in parallel on GPUs. Crucially, you can produce the rare and dangerous situations, like a dropped object, an unexpected collision, or a person walking into the workspace, which you'd almost never capture safely in the real world. You also get perfect labels for free: exact poses, contact points, segmentation, success or failure.

Of course, the big question has always been the sim-to-real gap. Early on, people found that policies trained purely in simulation broke when they met real friction, real sensor noise, and real visual messiness. But several things have gotten much better. Rendering is far more photorealistic. Physics engines handle contact and soft bodies better. And generative models can now create assets and even whole scenes at scale, so you aren't limited to what a team of artists can model by hand. Combined with techniques like domain randomization, the gap is narrowing to the point where synthetic data becomes the bulk of training, and real data becomes a calibration and grounding layer on top.

The way I see it is as a pyramid. At the base you have massive amounts of synthetic data that teach broad physical common sense and generalization. In the middle you have things like human videos, which show intent and task structure even without robot actions. At the top you have a smaller amount of high-quality real robot data that anchors everything to reality. If you try to build the whole pyramid out of the top layer alone, you never reach the scale needed for a general-purpose robot.

So for me, synthetic data isn't a shortcut or a substitute. It's the only realistic path I can see to giving embodied models the kind of data scale that made language models work. Whoever builds the best data engine, meaning the best loop between simulation, generation, and real-world feedback, will probably have a big advantage in this next phase.

r001.rationale: The response combines diverse synthetic scenarios with a smaller layer of high-quality real robot demonstrations, describing them as complementary parts of the training data.

r002.rationale: It does not compare reinforcement-learning problem setting to a teacher guiding students through questions.

r003.rationale: It says teleoperation data is costly and hard to scale, but does not identify narrowly staged teleoperation environments as a limit on generalization.

r004.rationale: It contrasts costly, slow real-world collection with virtual scenarios that can be varied freely and run in parallel on GPUs, conveying the shift from physical collection costs to compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that embodied intelligence has a data problem that looks nothing like the one language models had. When people trained large language models, the internet was already there. Decades of human writing, essentially free, already digitized. Robotics has no equivalent. There is no "internet of actions." Nobody has been recording, at scale, what a hand does when it picks up a cup, how much force it applies, how the wrist rotates, what it does when the cup is slippery.

So you look at the options. One is teleoperation, where a human drives a robot and you record everything. That data is high quality, but it is painfully expensive. You are paying a person to do one episode at a time, and a well-run lab might get a few thousand episodes a day across many stations. A model that needs to generalize across objects, lighting, kitchens, grips, and failure modes needs orders of magnitude more than that. The second option is internet video of humans, which is abundant but has a big embodiment gap. There are no action labels, the body is different, and you cannot measure contact.

Synthetic data, and by that I mean simulation plus generative models, fills the gap between those two. In a simulator you have perfect ground truth. Every pose, every contact force, every depth map comes for free. You can randomize textures, physics parameters, object shapes, camera positions, and generate millions of trajectories overnight at a cost that is essentially compute. Just as important, you can deliberately generate the long tail. The rare, dangerous, or awkward cases that a teleoperator would almost never encounter, like a glass tipping over or a drawer getting stuck, you can produce on purpose, thousands of times.

Now, the honest caveat is sim-to-real. Simulated physics is still not reality, especially for deformables, friction, and fine contact. So I do not think of synthetic data as a replacement for real data. I think of it as the thing that gives you the scale, and then a comparatively small amount of real-world data anchors the distribution and closes the gap. That ratio, large synthetic plus small real, is what makes the economics of scaling work at all. Without it you are stuck paying linearly for every new skill and every new environment, and that is a dead end for building generalist robots.

r001.rationale: It describes scenario diversity through randomized simulator conditions and rare cases, alongside high-quality human-driven teleoperation data and real-world data that anchors the distribution.

r002.rationale: It does not compare reinforcement-learning problem setting to a teacher guiding students through questions rather than demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It says teleoperation is costly and limited in volume, but does not identify narrowly staged teleoperation environments as a generalization limitation.

r004.rationale: It contrasts expensive teleoperation data with simulator data that costs compute, but does not explain replacing repeated rental of physical settings with virtual scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that embodied intelligence needs data about actions and their consequences. It’s not enough to recognize an object; a robot needs to learn what happens when it touches it, pushes it, or tries to pick it up. Collecting those interactions in the real world is slow and expensive, and some failures are dangerous to explore.

Synthetic data gives us a way to expand that experience. In simulation, we can vary objects, lighting, physical properties, and environments, and let a robot practice many versions of a task. We can also deliberately generate rare situations that might barely appear in real-world data but matter a lot for reliability.

The challenge is that a robot can become very good at the simulator without becoming good at the real task. So I see synthetic data as part of a loop: use real-world experience to identify what’s missing, generate useful variations, train, and then test on the physical robot. That loop is what makes it valuable for scaling—more experience, but grounded in what actually transfers.

r001.rationale: The response describes varied synthetic scenarios, but does not say good data combines scenario diversity with high-quality human demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It does not compare reinforcement learning problem-setting to a teacher guiding students with questions.

r003.rationale: It mentions real-world data collection costs, but not narrowly staged teleoperation environments or their effect on generalization.

r004.rationale: It says simulation expands experience when real-world collection is slow and expensive, but does not explain replacing rental costs for physical settings with compute costs for virtual scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that embodied intelligence needs data about actions and their consequences. It’s not enough to recognize an object; a robot has to learn what happens when it grasps it, pushes it, or encounters something unexpected. Collecting those interactions in the physical world is slow and expensive, and some failures are unsafe to repeat.

Synthetic data gives us a way to expand that experience. In simulation, we can vary objects, environments, and physical conditions, and generate examples of rare situations. We can also get precise labels that would be difficult to capture in the real world.

But the important question is whether that experience transfers. A large synthetic dataset is only useful if it helps the robot act better in reality. So I see real and synthetic data working together: real-world failures tell us what we’re missing, simulation lets us explore those cases at scale, and physical testing tells us whether we’ve actually improved.
